lawyer:
Md Osman Ghani, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Md Ohiullah, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Zafur Ali (Md) ------ Petitioner
vs
Chandpur Tea Co Ltd ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, was issued to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 11-8-1992 passed by the District Judge, Habiganj in Title Appeal No. 249 of 1989 (heard analogously with Title Appeal No. 250 of 1989) dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 19-9-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, Habiganj, in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, in decreeing the suit, should not be set aside.

2. It appears that one Chandpur Tea Co Limited, the opposite party No. 1, filed the instant suit on 30-1-1984, against the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 and the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite party Nos. 4 to 9, praying for a decree for declaration of title in the suit land and also for recovery of its possession, contending, inter alia, that the opposite party No. 1 is the owner of the suit land on obtaining lease from the Government. The said suit land was also recorded in the name of the opposite party No. 1 during the last settlement and survey operations. During the war of liberation in 1971, the defendants forcibly took possession of the suit land which is by the side of the main C & B road, however, after liberation the management of the opposite party No. 1, took possession of the suit land in 1974 but again in 1975 the defendants went into the possession of the lands mentioned in second schedule and constructed temporary huts and structures thereon. The officials of the opposite party No. 1 from time to time asked the defendants to vacate the suit land but instead, they filed a suit being the Title Suit No. 217 of 1980 in the Fourth Court of Munsif, Habiganj, praying for a decree for permanent injunction. The said suit was renumbered as the Title Suit No. 122 of 1985, on being transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, Habiganj. In the meantime, they raised further tin sheds in the suit land, as such, the opposite party No. 1 was constrained to file the instant suit, praying for a decree for declaration of its title in the suit land and for recovery of khas possession with a further declaration that the defendants have no right, title and interest in the suit land but were trespassers.

3. The petitioner, the defendant No. 2 and the defendant No. 3 filed a joint written statement while the other defendants filed another set of written statement in the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, denying all material allegations. Their case, in short, is that 30 years back, while one Mr Bruce was an assistant manager in the plaintiff-company, settled the suit land verbally with the defendants and since then they are in possession of the suit land by raising huts and tin-sheds.

4. The same contentions were raised by them in their earlier Title Suit No. 122 of 1985.

5. The learned Munsif, after hearing, decreed the suit.

6. On appeal, the learned District Judge affirmed the findings of the learned Munsif and dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved, the petitioner obtained the Rule.

7. The Rule was opposed on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 but without filing any counter-affidavit.

8. Mr Md Osman Ghani, Advocate, appears on behalf of the petitioner while Mr Md Alamin Sarker and Mr Md Ohiullah, Advocates, appear on behalf of the opposite party No. 1.

9. Mr Md Osman Ghani, Advocate, took me through the judgments of the Courts below and submits that the petitioner and others are in the suit land for more than last 50 years and since 1955 by constructing huts and other structures with the verbal permission from Mr Bruce, the Assistant Manager of the Tea Company and since 1955 they are in such possession. He further submits that the suit was filed in 1984 long after his title has been perfected by the principles of adverse possession that since the suit was filed beyond the period of limitation which was not taken into consideration by any of the courts below, thereby committed an error of law in the decision occasioning a failure of justice. The learned Advocate refers to the decisions in the case of Khondakar Mohiuddin vs Syed Moin Ahmed 28 DLR (AD) 85, Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman 44 DLR (AD) 100, Amanatullah vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan 2 MLR (AD) 239 = 2 BLC (AD) 134 and the case of Abdul Latif Chowdhury vs Md Nur Hossain 1997 BLD (AD) 230.

10. On the other hand, Mr Alamin Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, submits that firstly the suit is not barred by limitation since the petitioner entered into the possession in 1971 during the war of 1971 and was evicted there from some time after liberation but he again entered into possession in 1975 and, as such, the suit was filed well within the period of limitation in 1984. Secondly, he submits, even if it is accepted for argument's sake but without admitting it that he entered into the possession in 1955 by oral permission from an Assistant Manager of the plaintiff it would also not help the petitioner because of two reasons. i) The said Assistant Manager had no legal authority to give any such permission to occupy the properties of the Company and ii) secondly, the alleged prima facie possession of a squatter even if it is of 100 years, cannot allow the petitioner's claim of right by adverse possession. Besides Mr Sarker further submits that if it is admitted that he was in possession in 1971 even then by virtue of President's Order No. 12 of 1972 the period from 1-3-1971 to 1-3-1972, would be excluded for calculating the period of limitation of 12 years in 1984.

11. He further pointed out that the petitioner along with others, with the self-same contentions filed a separate suit for permanent injunction being Title Suit 217 of 1980 which on transfer to the Court of Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, was renumbered as the Title Suit No. 122 of 1985. The said suit was also heard analogously with the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 and was concurrently dismissed by both the Courts below and the Rule in respect of the said decree was also discharged earlier by another Bench of this Court. Under such circumstances, this Rule should also be discharged.

12. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides.

13. It appears that Chandpur Tea Co Limited filed the present suit praying, inter alia, for a decree for recovery of khas possession of the suit land. The suit land is situated by the side of the main road which is under the super-vision of the C&B Deptt of the Government. The present suit was filed by opposite party No. 1 on 30-1-1984. Earlier the petitioner and others filed a suit for permanent injunction against the opposite party No. 1 being Title Suit No. 217 of 1980, praying for a decree for temporary injunction. The said suit was also transferred to be tried along with the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, Habiganj, and both the suits were heard and disposed of analogously by the same judgment. The trial Court framed the following issues in respect of the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984:

(i)	Is the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 maintainable in its present form and manner?

(ii)	Is the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 properly valued and correct Court fees paid?

(iii)	Is the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, barred by the law of limitation?

(iv)	Has the plaintiff in the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, got right, title, interest in the suit land?

(v)	Is the plaintiff in the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 entitled to the decree for recovery of khas possession and other reliefs as prayed for?

14. The Issue Nos. V-VII were in respect of Title Suit No. 122 of 1985. The said suit is not the subject matter of this Rule, as such, those are not mentioned.

15. The plaintiff in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 examined two witnesses in support of its claim while the petitioner, one of the defendants, examined three witnesses in support of his claim.

16. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record found that the defendant-petitioner could not prove his claim that they raised the huts and other structures on receipt of alleged verbal permission from Mr Bruce either from 1955 or since 1964 or 1967. He also found that in his suit being Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 the petitioner did not claim any title by adverse possession rather their claim that they are in the suit land on oral permission from one Mr Bruce. But the claim of settlement of any land in their favour was neither averred nor found. As such, the learned Assistant Judge found that the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 or the defendant No. 2 in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, could not prove on evidence as to their claim of oral permission from the concerned authorities of the Chandpur Tea Estate Company Ltd on the basis of even oral permission from the said Opposite Party No. 1, as such, he found that the defendants in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, were not in legal possession of the suit land. On those findings the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 and decreed the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, allowing recovery of khas possession of the suit land.

17. On appeal, the learned District Judge also considered the evidence on record and found that the plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 and the defendants in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, could not prove any oral permission in their favour from the concerned authorities of the Chandpur Tea Company Ltd, and concurred with the findings of fact arrived at by the Assistant Judge. The learned District Judge also found that the President's Order No. 12 of 1972 allows deduction of the period from 1-3-1971 to 1-3-1972 in computing the period of limitation, as such, he found that even though the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 was filed in 1984 but it was within the period of limitation of 12 years.

18. We have also gone through the judgments of the Courts below and the evidence on record. The story of oral settlement in favour of the defendants was totally disbelieved by both the courts below. Besides the petitioner could not put forward any evidence before any of the Courts below, as to whether any Assistant Manager had any authority from the opposite-party-company to settle any land in favour of any person including the petitioner, as such, even if the petitioner obtained such verbal permission allegedly from Mr Bruce, it does not carry any legal right, as such, the possession of the petitioner allegedly from 1955 or from 1971, althrough was that of a squatter without any legal right whatsoever. The decisions which were referred to by Mr Osman Ghani, Advocate have got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of this case.

<u>19. It is apparent that the suit land is situated by the side of the land of C & Broad of the Government, at the periphery of the lands of the opposite party No. 1, as such, taking advantage of the situation of the land being far away from the main lands of the opposite party company and being by the side of the main road, the petitioner and other defendants raised their huts and structures including the tin-sheds, from time to time, without any lawful authority. As such, they do not have any semblance of any title whatsoever. They do not claim any right, by adverse possession. Besides, even if they are in possession since 1971, the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession, was within the period of limitation of 12 years under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, taking into consideration of the provisions of the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 12 of 1972). In that view of the matter, I find no reason to disagree with the concurrent findings of facts arrived at by both the Courts below.</u>

20. In that view of the matter, the judgment and decrees, passed by the Courts below are affirmed.

21. It appears that the petitioner is in illegal possession of the suit land for a very long time denying the right and possession of the opposite party company, the real owner, by raising frivolous claim of title, as such, a cost should be imposed.

22. Under the circumstances, the Rule should be discharged with cost.

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost all through.

24. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Send down the lower Court records below forthwith.

End.
